main.title: Ori and the Blind Forest
main.subtitle: Explore Nibel with Ori, Sein and abilities that reshape familiar paths
main.summary: Ori and the Blind Forest is a Metroidvania video game developed by Moon Studios and published by Microsoft Studios.

cards.heading: A spirit, a forest and a limited save
cards.text: Ori and the Blind Forest is a Metroidvania video game developed by Moon Studios and published by Microsoft Studios. The game was released for Windows and Xbox One in March 2015, and for Nintendo Switch in September 2019. Players assume control of Ori, a small white spirit, and Sein, the "light and eyes" of the Forest's Spirit Tree. Players are tasked to move between platforms and solve puzzles. The game features a save system called "Soul Links", which allows players to save their progress at will with limited resources, and an upgrade system that allows players to strengthen Ori's skills and abilities.

cards.heading: A studio working across borders
cards.text: The game was developed by Moon Studios, a collective organization without a set location. The distribution rights to the game were acquired by Microsoft a year after the beginning of the game's development. The game story was inspired by The Lion King and The Iron Giant, while some of the gameplay elements were inspired by the Rayman and Metroid franchises.

cards.heading: A celebrated debut and a direct sequel
cards.text: Upon release, the game received critical acclaim, with players praising the gameplay, art direction, story, action sequences, musical score, and environmental design. The game was also named as a title that represented art in video games. Moon Studios co-founder Gennadiy Korol said the game was profitable for the company within a few weeks after its initial launch. An expansion, called the Definitive Edition, was released in March 2016. A direct sequel, Ori and the Will of the Wisps, was announced during Electronic Entertainment Expo 2017 and was released on March 11, 2020.

cards.heading: Depth without a map
cards.text: Foreground branches, distant trunks and pools of light give Ori's woodland several visual layers. The playable path occupies only part of that space. What remains beyond reach matters too: it suggests a forest continuing outside the player's route, larger than the immediate challenge on screen.

cards.heading: Movement makes a landscape
cards.text: New abilities open routes through places Ori has already visited. A gap that previously stopped progress can become crossable, giving the player a reason to return to a remembered corner of the forest. Familiar landmarks help connect that new possibility to an earlier journey through the same area.

main.title: Mario Party 10
main.subtitle: Bowser gets the other screen
main.summary: Mario Party 10 is NDcube's Wii U party game, first released in Japan on 12 March 2015.

cards.heading: Bowser gets the other screen
cards.text: Mario Party 10 is NDcube's Wii U party game, first released in Japan on 12 March 2015. The main board mode continues Mario Party 9's shared vehicle and Mini Stars, while Bowser Party uses the GamePad to create a different contest. Four players cooperate against a fifth person controlling Bowser. The extra screen makes an opposing role possible within the same room, turning the familiar villain into another participant whose attention and controls differ from those of the group trying to escape.

cards.heading: Four players flee one pursuer
cards.text: In Bowser Party, the team travels together while Bowser pursues them and triggers special minigames. The GamePad provides the large character's viewpoint and input, while the other players react with their own controllers. The asymmetry gives a short challenge two sides: Bowser tries to exploit the situation, and the group must understand and survive it together. Losing health affects their continued journey, so cooperation extends beyond a single encounter. The player holding the separate screen becomes a continuing source of pressure along the board.

cards.heading: Three ways to use the party board
cards.text: Amiibo Party supplies another board format linked to figures, while the standard Mario Party mode keeps four competitors gathering Mini Stars across five maps. More than seventy minigames connect the different arrangements. Rei Kondoh and Toshiki Aida composed the music. The game explores several Wii U ideas at once, with Bowser Party making the clearest use of its unusual hardware: one person can remain physically beside the others while playing a visibly different part, using a private screen to challenge the shared television view.

main.title: Yakuza 0
main.subtitle: Kamurocho in 1988, Before the Legend
main.summary: Yakuza 0 places two young men inside the property deals, nightlife and criminal pressure of Japan in 1988.

cards.heading: A tiny plot of expensive land
cards.text: In December 1988, a small vacant plot interrupts a major redevelopment scheme in Kamurocho. Kazuma Kiryu, a twenty-year-old debt collector, becomes implicated in a killing. The supposedly empty land has owners, claimants and consequences. A property dispute gives the 2015 prequel a concrete reason for rival interests to collide.

cards.heading: Two cities, two young men
cards.text: Across the country in Osaka's Sotenbori district, twenty-four-year-old Goro Majima manages the Grand cabaret. His successful public role sits beside punishment and exclusion from the organisation he wants to rejoin. Moving between the two protagonists lets the same period appear through very different kinds of obligation.

cards.heading: Money makes the pressure visible
cards.text: SEGA's story places luxurious redevelopment beside people whose lives can be redirected by a single order. Kiryu's predicament begins with an ordinary collection job; Majima's apparent status does not give him freedom. That contrast makes the prequel more than a younger face for a familiar protagonist: each city gives ambition a price.

cards.heading: Arcades, side quests and Completion Points
cards.text: Players can freely walk around Kamurochō and Sotenbori, interacting with people they meet to trigger side-quests, battling enemies who attack them on the street, or playing several minigames, including fully playable versions of Sega arcade games such as Out Run, Super Hang-On, Space Harrier, and Fantasy Zone. Completing certain objectives, such as eating every dish at a restaurant or reaching a target score in a minigame, will also grant the player special Completion Point currency; these Completion Points can be spent at a shrine to receive additional bonuses, such as special items or character upgrades.

main.title: Code Name: S.T.E.A.M.
main.subtitle: Turn-Based Strategy from the Soldier's Shoulder
main.summary: Code Name: S.T.E.A.M. turns a limited third-person view and limited steam reserves into tactical decisions.

cards.heading: Lincoln recruits an unlikely squad
cards.text: An alien invasion meets an alternative nineteenth century powered by steam. Abraham Lincoln directs an unusual defensive force in Intelligent Systems' 2015 Nintendo 3DS game. Its comic-book presentation gives a strange collection of agents a common setting, while missions place a squad of four under the player's control.

cards.heading: A battlefield seen from the ground
cards.text: There is no overhead battlefield map to reveal everything at once. The third-person viewpoint makes scouting part of the turn: an agent must reach a useful position before the player can see what lies beyond it. Moving a soldier also changes the information available for the rest of the squad.

cards.heading: Keep something in reserve
cards.text: Both movement and weapon attacks consume steam. Spending the whole reserve can achieve more now, but holding some back permits an overwatch attack during the enemy's turn. Equipment and boilers alter those possibilities. A resource that sounds like period decoration becomes the link between positioning, attack and protection.

cards.heading: Comic-book art and Lovecraftian aliens
cards.text: Takao Sakai, the game's art director, explained that the art style was heavily influenced by the Silver Age of comic books, such as the works of Jack Kirby as well as more recent comic creators like Bruce Timm and Mike Mignola. The designs for the enemy alien characters were heavily influenced by the works of H. P. Lovecraft.
